newsitem.title: USA: Thai Yankee debut enjoys good reception in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Thai Yankee debut enjoys good reception in U.S.

text.p: The safe landing of the Kingdom of Thailand's debut Yankee bond was greeted with relief by analysts and traders in the United States.
The 10-year issue was priced late Thursday at 90 basis points over U.S. Treasuries, and the size of the issue was increased to $600 million from $500 million.
"The deal is well received," said Feroz Talyarkhan, head of Asian fixed-income research at Bear Stearns and Co. "It's positive for the Thai market."
The pricing was "on the generous side," even allowing for some negative impact from a Moody's downgrade, he said.
Moody's Investor's Service cut the kingdom's long-term foreign currency debt rating to A3 from A2, but Standard and Poor's maintained its single A rating.
At 90 basis points, the spread offered "great potential" for tightening in the secondary market, Talyarkhan said.
That assessment was shared by other analyst and traders. "If you look at the comparables in the market, the price is quite enticing for certain investors," said an analyst who requested anonymity.
Slovenia, which holds the same ratings as Thailand -- A3 by Moody's and single A by S&P -- has a five-year note traded at 50 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
Among other Southeast Asian sovereigns, Indonesia's 10-year bond -- rated Baa3 by Moody's and triple B by S&P -- was trading at 100 basis points over Treasuries.
"It's only 10 basis points tighter than Indonesia, which is rated three notches lower," the analyst said, referring to the Thai bond.
Even though the environment is cautious amid expectations of a further rise in U.S. interest rates, investors gave Thailand a fairly strong vote of confidence, a Eurobond trader said.
"People go for the sovereign credit," he said. "They feel comfortable that the Thai government would pay up."
The Thai deal was closely watched as a gauge of liquidity in the Yankee market, said another trader. "It showed that investors are still going after Yankees for yield pick-up (over domestic bonds)."
The Thai monetary authority is relying on high short-term interest rates to ward off speculative attacks on its currency, and tight credit has exacerbated the hardship on businesses.

Talyarkhan expected Thai interest rates to remain firm for three or four more months before returning to last summer's level. Pressure on rates should begin easing soon because the trends for macroeconomic improvements were already in place, he said.

Fears that the U.S. Federal Reserve will make more preemptive strikes against inflation apparently curtailed the appetite of investors for bonds with long maturity, as Thailand scrapped a 30-year tranche in favor of issuing only 10-year notes.
"I was surprised that they backed off," Talyarkhan said.
Judging from the steady tone of some 30-year bonds issued by high-quality banks in the market, a 30-year sovereign tranche could have placed without undue difficulty, he said.
